text: The back rank is nearly locked, with d3ふenze behind White's passed c3 and halfdraw passes toward the far square. Advancing h5 behind d3 sops the king but misses a direct capture to hold down White's inhibits coordination. The pawn advance is the simply exposing interposition: with the king on c5 beyond g5 and the b-stone gone and will éluombable defender, Black delivers the decisive blow. Any delay to take the 높 있는 pawn on c3 permits White to keorrow pawn and seal off the c-file, remaining eagle with only perimeter threats and no immediate mate available. So is it exb5? Actually the advanced pawnthreat is the underpromotion e2=O, capturing the pawn and attacking that fork. The pawn jumps to d2 after this, defensive force eliminates the pawn from accessing c3, and there the e2=O pawn secures a passed e2 pawn one move to exchange. So the move is exb5.

White has a rook on h1 and a bishop on b4 bearing down on the Black king on d8, but the bishop on b4 is already attacked by the rook on h1, so it cannot be captured. The rook on c2 is undefended and attacked by the rook on h1, so it is also available. The bishop on b4 can capture the undefended rook on c2, winning material and leaving Black with no immediate defense. After the capture, the rook on c2 is undefended and attacked by the rook on h1, so White plays Rxc2#, a checkmate. The king cannot escape to c8 because the rook on h1 covers that square, nor to c7 because the bishop on b4 controls it, nor to c9 because the rook on h1 covers that square, and d7 because the rook on h1 controls it. So the move is Rxc2#.

White has a pawn on g6 ready to promote, but the choice of piece is critical. Promoting to a queen with g7+ gives check, but Black can immediately recapture the queen with the rook on c2, winning material and leaving White without a winning advantage. Promoting to a rook with g1+ also gives check, but Black can recapture the rook with the queen, again winning material. The knight on g6 attacks h6, and the black king on h6 is completely boxed in by its own pawns on h7 and g8, with no escape squares. So the move is Nxh6#.

White has a rook on f4 and a pawn on h6, but the black king on h5 is dangerously exposed. Rxf1+ gives check but the king simply steps to g6 and escapes, leaving White without a forced continuation. Rf5+ also gives check, but the king can flee to g6 and the attack dissipates. The key is to push the h-pawn to g7, giving check to the king on h5. The king cannot go to g6 because the rook on f4 covers that square, and the king cannot go to g4 because the pawn on h6 controls it. The rook on f4 then captures the rook on g7, winning material and leaving Black with no immediate reply. So the move is hg7+.

The rook slides to g1 delivering immediate checkmate, as the white king on g2 is completely boxed in by its own pawns on f2 and c4, while the rook on h1 controls the h-file and the queen on d2 covers the g2 escape. The rook's path to g1 is unobstructed, and the queen's presence on d2 seals off any flight to the d-file. This is the fastest and most decisive finish, exploiting the mating net created by the rook's advance.

The white king on e1 is completely trapped with its own pieces blocking every other flight square and half the board sealed off. Qxf2+ gives check but White captures back and the king finds a safe square, so the attack runs out of steam. Nxf2+ is a check too, but White simply recaptures and the king escapes to the center. The right idea is to first push the bishop from f8 to e6, delivering check to the king while simultaneously cutting the g2 square with the queen. The king has no legal move: e2 is attacked by the new bishop and the pawn on e4 is pinned to the king by the queen, g1 and g2 are covered by the knight on g4, and f1 is blocked by the bishop on f1. So the move is Be6#.

The queen slides to h5, delivering immediate checkmate by attacking the h7 pawn and the rook on g8, while the knight on c3 and pawns on b3 and c2 seal off the king's escape routes. The rook on g8 and the bishop on c6 are too far away to intervene. This mate is the most efficient continuation of the forced sequence, exploiting the queen's reach and the pawn's advance.

White has a queen on f6 and a rook on h2, while Black's king sits exposed on g8 with the queen on d8 and rook on h8 nearby. Qxf7+ gives check but the king simply captures the queen, and after the king escapes the mating net is lost. Qxg6+ wins a pawn but the king can step away and the attack fizzles. The rook on h2 can slide to h7, delivering checkmate: the king on g8 cannot go to f8 because the queen on f6 covers that square, cannot go to f7 because the queen on f6 covers it, cannot go to g7 because the rook on h2 controls that square, and cannot go to h8 because the rook on h2 controls it. So the move is Rh7#.

The rook slides to h1 delivering immediate checkmate, as the white king on h2 is hemmed in by its own pawns on g2 and h3, the queen on d5, and the bishop on e5. The rook's path to h1 is unobstructed, and the queen's presence on d5 covers the h1 square, while the f2 and g6 pawns seal off f1 and g1. This mate is the fastest and most direct conclusion to the position, exploiting the tight structure of the white king's corner.

White has a rook on e8 bearing down on e1. The Closed anfions are Kc4, gxf6, and a dangerous recomposition driven by Bc4, so no piece is to do this straightforward material risk. Consider Ne4+, forcing the king to check, but Rxe8 opens a command path and no forced mate follows. Keeping the rook under constant target moveslets White do sommeorts with black pins on f7. Starting as Baker Rxd5 works out but triggers premature predations and gives up the rook for the Black pawn on c4 without winning anything. The rook can instead decide on an immediate mate by moving to e1: that rook capture strips the black knight and rook neutralizes both, and the king has nowhere to flee—the pawn on f6 is stuck in front, Sof2 usups rook checks, middle-rook checks, and the pawn blocks the f7 exit—wreaving Tch6#. So the move is Ra1#.

Black needs to act decisively to turn the tide. Grabbing the b-pawn with check fails immediately, giving White time to reorganize and keep the initiative. Kd6 merely slides the king a square without giving mate, letting White's king find a defensive position. The key observation is that the g2 pawn stands in the way of White's checkmate on the kingside, since it is blocked by the black pawn on g4 and cannot prevent the attack. After Black moves the f-pawn to f3, the g2 pawn captures it, eliminating the obstruction while simultaneously proclaiming that the check from e6 is forced, as the rook on e6 is available and the honeycomb mates instantly. So the move is f3.

The rook slides to c8 delivering immediate checkmate, as the queen on c6 covers the g8 escape square and the rook on c8 controls the g8 and h8 squares, while the rook on g6 covers g7 and the queen on e6 covers f7. The black king on g8 has no flight squares, and the rook on c1 and g6 seal off the remaining escape routes. This is the fastest and most direct mate, making Rg7 the only legal move to prepare the check.

Black has a knight on b8 and a pawn on e7, but the real prize is the undefended knight on f3. White's king on g1 is hemmed in by its own pawns on g3 and f2, and the queen on d1 is too far away to intervene. Nxf3# captures the knight with check, and the king cannot escape: the queen on d1 cannot reach f3, the knight on g3 is blocked by its own pawn, and the rook on f1 is pinned to the king by the knight on f3. So the move is Nxf3#.

White's queen on f3 and bishop on g3 are already aimed at the black king on c8, but the king has multiple flight squares and the position is not yet decided. Qxd5+ wins a pawn but the king escapes to d7 or d8, and the attack loses momentum. Qxf6+ also wins a pawn but the king can step to d7 or d8, and the bishop on g3 remains undefended. The key is that the bishop on g3 is attacked by the queen on f3 and the knight on c3, and the king on c8 cannot capture the bishop because the queen covers the entire c8 square. So the move is Qxg6#.

The rook slides to h2 delivering immediate checkmate, as the knight on f3 covers g1 and h2, while the pawn on f2 and c3 block the escape squares. The rook's path to h2 is unobstructed, and the knight's control of g1 and h2 ensures the king has no flight squares. This completes the forced mate from the rook's advance, making the move h1 the only winning continuation.

White has a pawn on f2 ready to promote, but the black king on g8 is dangerously exposed. Promoting to a queen with f1=Q looks tempting, but Black can immediately capture the new queen with the rook, winning the initiative. Promoting to a rook with f1=R is also not enough: Black can simply recapture the rook with the queen, and the king escapes to safety. The key is to promote to a knight first: f1=N+ gives check, forcing the king to g7. The knight then leaps to h7, delivering checkmate—the king has no escape squares, and the rook on e2 covers the g8 square. So the move is f1=N+.

The queen slides to h2 delivering immediate checkmate, as the white king on h1 is hemmed in by its own pawns on h2 and f4, while the rook on c1 and pawn on g7 block escape routes. The queen's path to h2 is unobstructed, and the white king has no flight squares. This is the fastest and most direct mate, exploiting the queen's reach and the pawns' support. Other options like h4 or h3 would allow White to prolong the game, but h2# ends it immediately.

Black has a queen on e1 and a bishop on g5 bearing down on the White king on h2, but the king is trapped in the corner with no escape. Qxg2+ captures the pawn on g2 with check, but White can recapture the queen and the king escapes to safety. Qxe2+ also gives check, but White can recapture the queen and the king slips away. The winning move is to slide the queen to e1, where it attacks the king directly along the first rank and the bishop on g2 covers g2, leaving the king with no legal move. So the move is Qe1#.

White has a pawn on f4 ready to promote, but the choice of piece matters. Promoting to a queen with h8=Q looks powerful, but Black's queen on e8 and bishop on d6 can immediately capture the new queen, winning it for free. Promoting to a rook with h8=R is also insufficient: Black's queen on e8 and bishop on d6 can capture the rook, again winning material. The key is to promote to a knight first: the knight on f4 attacks the undefended black king on f7, and the king cannot capture because the knight on f4 is not covered by the queen on h5. So the move is f4=N#.

White has a knight on d6 and a rook on g1 bearing down on the Black king on h8, but the king is completely trapped: the rook on g1 covers g7, the bishop on g7 covers g8, and the knight on d6 controls h7. The alternative Ng5+ gives check but the king simply escapes to g8, and the mating net dissolves. The rook on g1 can instead slide to h1, delivering checkmate: the king cannot go to g8 (covered by the bishop on g7), cannot go to g7 (covered by the bishop on g7), cannot go to h7 (covered by the knight on d6), and cannot go to g8 (covered by the rook on g1). So the move is Rh1#.

White has a pawn on f2 ready to promote, but the choice of piece matters. Promoting to a queen with f1=Q looks tempting, but Black's queen on f5 can immediately capture the new queen, winning it outright. Promoting to a rook with f1=R is also not enough: Black's queen on f5 can capture the rook on f1, again winning material. The key is to promote to a knight first: f1=N+ gives check, forcing the king to g7. The knight then captures the queen on f5 with check, and the king is forced to g8, after which the knight on f1 delivers checkmate. So the move is f1=N+.

White has a queen on h4 and a knight on b3 bearing down on the Black king on h8, but the king is completely trapped: the rook on g4 covers g8, the rook on g8 controls g7, the pawn on g6 blocks g7, and the knight on b3 covers g8. The queen can deliver immediate checkmate by landing on h7, since the king cannot escape to g8, g7, or h8. The alternative Qg3+ would allow the king to capture the queen, prolonging the game. Qh7# is the cleanest and fastest finish.

White has a knight on e4 and a bishop on g5 bearing down on the Black king on e8, while the queen on d2 is active. The immediate Qxd7+ wins the bishop but lets Black recapture with the queen, and the king escapes to safety. Qxf4+ also wins a pawn but Black can recapture with the queen, and the king slips away. The knight on e4 can instead leap to f6, giving check to the king on e8 while the bishop on g5 covers f7 and g8, and the queen on d2 controls d8 and e7. The king has no legal escape, so the move is Nf6#.

The rook slides to f5 delivering immediate checkmate, as the rook controls the entire fifth rank and the black king on f7 is hemmed in by its own pawns on f5 and g7. The rook on f6 and the rook on c7 block any escape routes, while the pawns on g7 and f5 seal off those squares. The e7 pawn supports the queen's advance to e8, but the mate is immediate and unstoppable. This is the fastest and most direct mate in the position.

White has a queen on d2 and a bishop on c1, while Black's queen on f6 and rooks on a5 and f8 dominate the position. Qxf6+ gives check but Black can recapture the queen, and the king escapes to safety. Qxd6 wins a pawn but Black's queen on f6 remains active and the attack stalls. The bishop on c1 can instead leap to h6, delivering check to the king on g8. The king has no escape: the queen on d2 covers g7 and h7, the rook on a1 controls a8, and the bishop on h6 covers g7. So the move is Bh6#.

White has a rook on e1 bearing down on d1. One option is Nh4, a quiet rook sacrifice that allows Rxe5, but then d1 would fall under check from the c3-rook and the winning material balance collapses entirely. Moving the knight toward d5, Nxd5, removes the black's central defender but lets it retain dangerous counterplay: Rxe2+ is easy and the game runs far longer with a forced e1-d5+ Qxg2 Kg1 to win back tempo. Nh4+ is also a forcing rook, yet instead Kf8# delivers an immediate checkmate, with the bishop on c3 covering g7. So the move is Nh4+.

White has a knight on b1 and a bishop on c4, but the black knight on d5 is pinned to the king by the bishop on e7, so it cannot move. The bishop on c4 can capture the pinned knight with check, and the king has no escape: the rook on a1 and the pawn on a2 block the king's flight squares, and the knight on b1 covers g7. The alternative Nxd5 would allow Black to recapture the knight with the bishop, winning material and leaving White without a forced mate. So the move is Bxd5#.

The queen slides to d3 delivering immediate checkmate, as the white king on f3 is boxed in by its own pawns on f2 and g5, while the queen covers d2 and d4, and the pawn on g5 controls g4. The queen's path to d3 is unobstructed, and the king has no escape squares. This is the fastest and most direct mate, making it the strongest move in the position.

The white bishop on d2 sits undefended and has no king or pawn blocking it. An immediate capture is impossible because the rook on a5 cannot reach b2 without being checkered on the a5–c5 diagonal. Instead, a king step to h4 leaves White time to take the rook with the bishop on b2, clearing the diagonal entirely. With the bishop gone and the rook on b1 undefended, Rb1# delivers checkmate as the only remaining legal move. So the move is Kh4.

White has two rooks and a rook on c6, while Black's rooks on f4 and g4 are dangerously close to the White king on h3. Rc5+ gives check but the king simply steps away and the attack dissipates. Rc4+ also gives check, but the king can flee to g4 and the rook on c6 is no longer in the game. The winning idea is to slide the rook from c6 to h6, delivering checkmate: the king on g5 is covered by the rook on c6, the rook on f4 is pinned to the king by the rook on c6, and the Black king on g4 cannot reach h6 because the rook on c6 controls that square. So the move is Rh6#.

White has a rook on f1 bearing down on d1 while the Black king on c8 is hemmed in by its own pawns on b6, d7, and e6. Rxc1+ gives check but the king simply steps away and there is no forced mate. Bg3+ also checks but the king escapes to e7 and the mating net dissolves. The rook on d1 slides to d8 and the king cannot run: b7 is blocked by a pawn, b8 is occupied by its own rook, b6 and c7 are both covered by the bishop on d6 along the d-file, c8 is controlled by both the rook on d1 and the bishop on c4, while a7, d7, d8, and e8 are all covered by the Black rooks on d8 and h8. No piece can interpose or capture the rook, so the combination ends immediately. So the move is Rd8#.

The rook slides to c2 delivering immediate checkmate, as the rook covers the entire c-file and the black king on d6 is hemmed in by its own pawn on d4 and the pawn on a6. The rook's path to c2 is unobstructed, and the black rook on c2 is pinned to the c-file by the rook on c7. The pawn on a6 blocks the a6 escape, while the pawn on d4 and the black pawn on d4 seal off d6. This mate is the fastest and most direct continuation of the rook's long-range attack.

The rook slides to f7 delivering immediate checkmate, as the rook on f7 attacks the black king on f8 while the rook on g7 covers g8 and the pawn on g6 blocks g7. The black rook on e8 and pawns on h5 and c6 are irrelevant to the mating net. This is the fastest and most direct mate, exploiting the rook's reach and the pawn's support.

The rook slides to d8 delivering immediate checkmate, as the queen on f4 covers d8 and the rook on d4 controls d7 and d6, while the knight on e3 and bishop on g2 seal off the escape squares. The white king on f1 is completely trapped by its own pawns on f2 and g5, and the queen on f4 covers the f2 square, leaving no flight. This is the fastest and most decisive finish, exploiting the rook's direct path to d8.

White has a queen on a7 and rooks on c1 and f1, while Black's king sits exposed on c8 with the queen on f3 and rooks on d8 and g8. Qxc7+ gives check but the king simply steps away and the attack fizzles. Qxd7+ also gives check, but the king escapes to d7 or d8 and the mating net dissolves. The rook on c1 can slide to c7, delivering checkmate: the king on c8 cannot go to d8 (occupied by the rook), d7 (occupied by the bishop), or d8 (occupied by the rook), and d7 and d8 are both covered by the queen on a7. So the move is Rc7#.

The rook slides to h7 delivering immediate checkmate, as the queen on d8 covers g8 and h8, the knight on f6 covers g8 and h8, and the rook on h8 controls h7. The black king on g7 is completely trapped with no escape squares. This is the fastest and most direct mate, exploiting the rook's reach and the queen's coverage of the g-file.

Black has a pawn on g6 ready to promote, but the choice of piece matters. Promoting to a queen with g5+ gives check, but White can simply recapture the g-pawn with the king, and the promotion is not forced. Promoting to a rook with g5+ also gives check, but White can recapture the rook with the king, again leaving the promotion undefended. The key is that the g-pawn promotes to a knight on g5, delivering check to the king on d3. The king cannot go to d2 because the knight on g5 covers that square, and d4 is occupied by White's own pawn. The king on e2 is also covered by the knight on g5, and the king cannot step to f3 because the pawn on f4 attacks it. So the move is g5#.

White has a pawn on e5 and a queen on g6, but the black king on b7 is dangerously exposed. Qxg4+ wins a pawn with check, but the king escapes to c8 and the attack fizzles. Qxc7+ also wins a rook with check, but the king simply steps away and the attack runs out of steam. The key is that the queen on g6 can leap to f7, delivering checkmate: the king on b7 cannot go to c8 because the queen covers that square, cannot go to c7 because the rook on c7 is pinned to the king, and cannot go to d7 because the pawn on d7 is guarded by the queen on f7. So the move is Qf7#.

The pawn on f4 is ready to promote, and the pawn on b3 is pinned to the king on d4 by the pawn on a5, while the pawn on a4 covers the b5 square. Promoting to a queen is the only legal move, as the pawn on f4 is the only one that can reach the promotion square. The queen then delivers immediate checkmate by moving to f7, covering the f5 pawn and the b6 square, while the king on d4 controls d5 and e5, and the pawn on a4 covers b5. The white king on h6 is completely trapped with no escape.

The knight leaps to b7, checking the king on a6. The attack is immediate and decisive: no escape squares exist along the kingside once the attack is established, and the black pieces are all controlled by the knight and pinned by the rook on h8. This direct check gives White full force before the king can regroup. Raxh3+ also delivers a check with check, but that king can capture the rook and slip away, reducing the tension. Ne4, another check, delays the blow but hands the king a flight path toward the center that slows the White victory. This check finishes the attack cleanly because the king has no legal reply anywhere. So the move is b7#.

The queen captures on c8 with check, forcing the white king to g1. The rook on c1 and the queen on c8 control the c1 square, while the rook on d8 and the queen on f8 cover the d8 and f8 squares, respectively. The knight on e8 and the pawns on f2 and g2 seal off the remaining escape routes. The queen's path to c8 is now unobstructed, and the rook on c1 and the queen on c8 together deliver immediate checkmate.

The queen slides to c3 delivering immediate checkmate, as the rook on h8 and the knight on b6 seal off the king's escape routes. The queen's path to c3 is unobstructed by any black pieces, and the knight on b6 covers d8, d7, and e7, while the rook on f1 controls e1 and d1. The pawns on c5 and d5 block the king's flight to those squares, and the pawn on e6 and the pawn on f7 prevent any retreat. This mate is the fastest and most direct conclusion to the position, making a4c3 the decisive move.

White's queen on g5 dominates and is perfectly placed for a finishing blow. Qxg6+ gives check, but Black's king simply escapes to e8 and the attack stalls. Nd5 attacks the king on e8 but also leaves the rooks free to march past d7. However, once Black's f3-rush forces a rook on g3 and the king moves to e8, the rook on f3 seals off the f-file while the queen on g5 attacks g8 directly and f7 where the queen sits. So the move is Qxf3+. The king cannot escape because g8 is attacked, g6 is covered along the seventh rank, and f7 holds the f3-rook captive. All other king escapes also fall silent. Therefore, Qxf3+ is the force-movement finish.

The queen slides to c6 delivering immediate checkmate, as the knight on d7 and rook on d8 block the escape squares while the queen covers c8 and the rook on h4 controls h8. The black king has no flight squares and no piece can interpose. This is the fastest and most direct mate, exploiting the queen's reach and the pawns' support on c6.

Black has a pawn on f6 ready to promote, but the choice of piece matters. Promoting to a queen with f5=Q looks powerful, but White can immediately capture the new queen with the king, winning the piece for free. Promoting to a rook with f5=R also gives check, but White can simply recapture the rook with the king, eliminating the new piece and keeping the material balance. The key is to promote to a knight first: f5=N+ gives check, forcing the king to e2, and then the knight on f5 covers e1 and e2, while the pawn on g5 controls g4, leaving the king with no legal move. So the move is f5=N+.

Black has a queen on b2 and a rook on e8, while White's king on f1 is hemmed in by its own pieces. Qxf6+ gives check but White can capture the queen with the king, escaping the mating net. Qxg3+ wins a pawn but White recaptures and the king slips away. The rook on e8 can slide to e1, delivering checkmate: the king on f1 cannot go to g1 (covered by the rook), g2 (covered by the queen on b2), or h1 (covered by the rook on e1), and no White piece can interpose or capture the rook. So the move is Re1#.

Black has a rook on b8 and a bishop on a4 bearing down on the White king on c3, while the White queen on h8 is far from the action. Rxh8+ gives check but the king simply steps away and the attack stalls. Rb3+ also gives check, but the king can flee to d2 and the attack loses momentum. The winning idea is to slide the rook from b8 to c8, delivering checkmate: the king on c3 cannot go to b3 (covered by the rook on b8), d2 is controlled by the rook on b8, and d1 is covered by the rook on b2. The White queen on h8 is too far to intervene. So the move is Rc8#.

Black's king sits on e7 with the c4 pawn ready to promote, while White's king on h5 is dangerously exposed. Promoting to a queen with c4=Q looks tempting, but White immediately captures the new queen with the rook, winning it for free. Moving the king to f8 is also insufficient: White simply captures the c4 pawn with the rook, keeping the queen on the board and leaving Black without a decisive advantage. The key is to advance the pawn to c5, which attacks the king on h5 and forces it to move. The king is then forced to g5, and Black plays c6, a rook check that drives the king to h4, after which the queen captures on g6, winning the rook for a queen. So the move is c5.

The queen slides to h4 delivering immediate checkmate, as the rook on f8 and pawn on h4 seal the escape squares while the bishop on f5 covers h7 and the queen covers h7 and h6. The black king on h6 has no flight squares, and the queen's path to h4 is unobstructed. This is the fastest and most direct mate, exploiting the queen's reach and the black king's cramped position.

Black has a bishop on b4 and a rook on h8 bearing down on the White king on d1, but the king is already in check from the rook on e1. The tempting Bxg2 wins a pawn but allows White to recapture the bishop with the rook, and the king escapes to safety. The rook on e1 is completely undefended: the bishop on b4 covers e1, the rook on h8 covers e2, and the king on d1 is attacked by the rook on h8. So the move is Rxe1#.
